items.title: A Lover’s Quarrel with the World
items.author: Elif Shafak
items.quote: A poem begins as a lump in the throat, a sense of wrong, a homesickness, a lovesickness. It is a reaching-out expression; an effort to find fulfillment.
items.hook: How literature is born from a wound.

items.title: Every Heart Sings an Incomplete Song
items.author: Elif Shafak
items.quote: In the face of death and destruction, all differences had evaporated. There was not a single soul that the grocer scowled at that night.
items.hook: A moment of unity in the face of an earthquake reveals the power of shared humanity.

items.title: Home Is A Place Where You Have Never Been
items.author: Elif Shafak
items.quote:
‘You… you traveled to Istanbul on the trail of an imaginary character ?”‘
‘Yup, we even went to the Cemetery of the Companionless.’
items.hook: Discover how a novel inspired a journey to Istanbul and redefined the concept of home.

items.title: Hope is the Last Thing that Remains
items.author: Elif Shafak
items.quote: Perhaps we are right in putting hope into our novels, our stories and our poems. Perhaps this is how we resist and rebel, for we know, or we sense, intuitively rather than intellectually, that hope, such an essential source for humanity, needs literature to survive and thrive.
items.hook: How literature preserves hope in times of crisis

items.title: What Is “a Character,” Anyway?
items.author: George Saunders
items.quote: The essence of a character comes, for me, during revision, as the language gets tighter and the character starts sounding more like themselves, i.e., telling me more clearly who they are.
items.hook: Discover how characters can emerge organically in writing.

items.title: A Little Hope
items.author: James Crews
items.quote:
I held the hydrangeas under the hose
and watched a few white crab spiders
skitter out of the interlocking blossoms,
and down my hand. Untouched by
their beauty, by the amplified buzzing
of a bumblebee rolling inside the pollen-
rich cup of a windflower, I was tired
of news unspooling everything that’s wrong
with the world, weary of endless lies.
items.hook: Finding hope in nature amidst a world filled with negativity.

items.title: Allowed To Be Ordinary
items.author: James Crews
items.quote:
When I stop comparing and allow myself
to be ordinary—folding tea towels
and T-shirts into neat squares, rinsing out
the sticky jar that once held honey—I taste
a piece of eternity.
items.hook: Discover the holiness in everyday tasks.

items.title: Gathering Mint
items.author: James Crews
items.quote: Yet as I knelt on the ground that afternoon, it occurred to me that we humans almost always build our lives between bloom and ruin.
items.hook: Finding grounding in nature amidst life's uncertainties.

items.title: In Dark Times
items.author: James Crews
items.quote:
What I’m trying to say is that you have
no idea what kind of night someone
might be holding inside, and a single
soft word …
items.hook: Discover the unseen burdens we carry and the power of a soft word.

items.title: Teranga
items.author: James Crews
items.quote: It is shared, it is for both of us—the gift flowing back and forth in all directions to touch the lives of strangers who were never a part of the initial exchange, caressing their skin like steady rain in the middle of a drought, making them look up at the sky with unshielded eyes, seeing now: to give is also to receive.
items.hook: Rethink gratitude with Senegal's teranga: 'It is shared, it is for both of us.'

items.title: Fake thinking and real thinking
items.author: Joe Carlsmith
items.quote: Map vs. world: Is my mind directed at an abstraction, or it is trying to see past its model to the world beyond?
items.hook: Explore the spectrum of 'fake vs. real' thinking

items.title: How I start a new book
items.author: Katherine May
items.quote:
Chase down your ideas
The very beginnings of my writing projects are marked mainly by exhaustive reading. The actual writing is surprisingly thin on the ground. Instead, I make an attempt to know absolutely everything about the topic in hand, hunting down every book, article, film and interview on my subject, making transcripts where I need them, and copying quotes and ideas into my notebook.
items.hook: Discover Katherine May's unique approach to starting a new book.

items.title: How to keep a writer’s notebook
items.author: Katherine May
items.quote: My notebook is made for nobody’s eyes but my own. It’s a completely private space, and I protect that viciously.
items.hook: Discover the unruly art of keeping a writer's notebook.

items.title: How to light the dark months
items.author: Katherine May
items.quote: Lighting winter is an art and a daily practice, an act of survival and a gesture of love.
items.hook: Embrace winter's unique beauty through the art of lighting.

items.title: What it's like to grow up autistic
items.author: Katherine May
items.quote: I believed that at some point, when I figured it out, I would take my own life. I had no plan for adulthood at all; I didn’t think I needed to choose a career because I didn’t expect to be there.
items.hook: Understanding life as an autistic person without support

items.title: Botflies, Blowflies, and Other Parasites
items.author: Laura Erickson
items.quote: The scientists found that in every single nest, the fur was contaminated with at least 2 pesticides—in some, as many as 11—each one in common veterinary use to protect livestock and pets. But are these pesticides actually dangerous for birds? The researchers discovered that the more of these pesticides present in the fur incorporated into a nest, the fewer eggs produced and the higher the chick mortality.
items.hook: Discover how treated pet fur in bird nests can harm more than it helps.

items.title: Forget Forgetfulness
items.author: Laura Erickson
items.quote: Whether in an oak tree or on the ground below, Blue Jays sort through acorns, selecting the most viable ones to store away.
items.hook: Discover why Blue Jays are strategic acorn hoarders, not forgetful.

items.title: O frabjous day! Callooh! Callay!
items.author: Laura Erickson
items.quote: I needed these babies to survive. Of course, as they grew independent and I could no longer recognize them, they became regular old Pileated Woodpeckers. But BB was still my BB!
items.hook: Discover the emotional bond between a woman and a Pileated Woodpecker.

items.title: Piping Plovers Nest on Wisconsin Point!
items.author: Laura Erickson
items.quote: Captive rearing has been used in the Great Lakes since 1992 to salvage eggs that would otherwise have no chance of survival after a nest is abandoned, usually because one of the parents is killed or high water floods the nest.
items.hook: Discover how habitat restoration brought Piping Plovers back to Wisconsin Point.

items.title: Seasonal Transitions
items.author: Laura Erickson
items.quote: The birds themselves, both as individuals and as species, see seasonal transitions with much more nuance.
items.hook: Discover how birds mark the transition from summer to autumn with nuanced precision.

items.title: The Tiniest Bird in the Universe
items.author: Laura Erickson
items.quote: The tiny Bee Hummingbird is called the zunzúncito (meaning tiny zunzún) by Cubans.
items.hook: Discover the world of the tiniest bird and its ecological wonders.

items.title: Pep Talk
items.publication: For Dear Life with Maggie Smith
items.author: Maggie Smith
items.quote: Poems may not change the world directly, but a poem can change a person who can change the world. —Richard Blanco
items.hook: Writing and poetry's significance in challenging times

items.title: John Gray on why "progress" in politics is an illusion
items.author: Jonny Thomson
items.quote: Progress is not the same as improvement. Progress means a cumulative advance that does not unwind over generations or centuries.
items.hook: Is progress in politics and ethics an illusion?

items.title: How to master your moods
items.author: Jonny Thomson
items.quote: Your moods define how you perceive the world. They define how you remember the world. Your moods define what the world even means.
items.hook: Explore how moods shape your perception of the world.

items.title: One of the cruelest things to tell any child
items.author: Jonny Thomson
items.quote: A society is just when it supports everyone’s capabilities to that threshold.
items.hook: Explore how denying beauty and creativity can be a profound injustice.

items.title: You're gambling every time you trust someone
items.author: Jonny Thomson
items.quote: The world is unpredictable, and the people in it are even worse. The art of living is about getting used to uncertainty and ignorance. Are we alone in the universe? Maybe.
items.hook: Trust is a gamble: navigating uncertainty in relationships.

items.title: The Louis Theroux Effect
items.author: Jonny Thomson
items.quote: To change your inner life, you have to change your outer life. In the modern psychological lexicon, we talk about behavioral activation or self-perception theory, but this idea appears far earlier than that. It was there 2,500 years ago in China.
items.hook: How watching Louis Theroux changed my listening and thinking.

items.title: The unspoken rules of how and where to think
items.author: Jonny Thomson
items.quote: The tap in the shower never worked properly. The on-off side was fine, but the hot-cold one lived by its own chaotic rulebook.
items.hook: Explore the difference between shallow and deep solutions in life.

items.title: Three questions to ask to find out if its really love
items.author: Jonny Thomson
items.quote: Rinpoche argues that there is a difference between attachment and love. Attachment is when we cling to another person. We get possessive of them. We get jealous. We don’t give them space. But for Rinpoche, love is something else entirely.
items.hook: Discover the Buddhist perspective on love versus attachment.

items.title: The Assault on the Roadless Rule, and how you can get involved.
items.author: Nerdy About Nature
items.quote: The more funding available for the forest service, parks, and public services, the more resources are available to prevent these fires from occurring in the first place, and help stop their spread if they do start.
items.hook: How rescinding the Roadless Rule threatens forests and communities.

items.title: Charlie Smith's "The Rose"
items.publication: Ordinary Plots: Meditations on Poems + Verse
items.author: Devin Kelly
items.quote: I'm almost naked here, skinnier than I used to be, almost helpless or maybe I'm completely helpless as the religious say is the way to heaven—all right I'm helpless—
items.hook: Explore the vulnerability and searching wonder in Charlie Smith's 'The Rose.'

items.title: Claudia Emerson's "Metaphor"
items.publication: Ordinary Plots: Meditations on Poems + Verse
items.author: Devin Kelly
items.quote: Isn’t that what today’s poem does? Isn’t that what a metaphor does? It takes the seeming-smallness of a moment—a bat flying through a house—and makes it worth the whole universe. It makes what once was trivial related, now, to everything.
items.hook: How metaphors transform ordinary moments into universal truths.

items.title: Jennifer Grotz’s “Over and Above”
items.publication: Ordinary Plots: Meditations on Poems + Verse
items.author: Devin Kelly
items.quote: I attended the summer rain. When it pelted the lake like fingers across a keyless piano, I attended the fingertips’ perforations on the soft surface.
items.hook: Discover how 'attended' transforms in poetry to mean more than presence.

items.title: Kyle Carrero Lopez’s “Performance Studies”
items.publication: Ordinary Plots: Meditations on Poems + Verse
items.author: Devin Kelly
items.quote: Every act of being in front of others is an act of performance, and so, to choose to be yourself in such a moment is an honest choice at the heart of such a performance.
items.hook: Exploring the authenticity and politics of performance through poetry.

items.title: Linda Pastan's "Imaginary Conversation"
items.publication: Ordinary Plots: Meditations on Poems + Verse
items.author: Devin Kelly
items.quote: But why the last? I ask. Why not live each day as if it were the first— all raw astonishment, Eve rubbing her eyes awake that first morning, the sun coming up like an ingénue in the east?
items.hook: Rethinking time: live each day as if it were your first.

items.title: Margaret Draft's "Colic"
items.publication: Ordinary Plots: Meditations on Poems + Verse
items.author: Devin Kelly
items.quote:
You hollow out the land,
you try to make enough space, and when you think you have enough,
keep digging.
items.hook: Exploring loss and memory through the metaphor of horses.

items.title: Marie Howe's "Hurry"
items.publication: Ordinary Plots: Meditations on Poems + Verse
items.author: Devin Kelly
items.quote: And, Hurry up, she says, over her shoulder, looking back at me, laughing.
items.hook: Exploring the profound connections in Marie Howe's poetry through the word 'and'.

items.title: Mary Oliver's "Clam"
items.publication: Ordinary Plots: Meditations on Poems + Verse
items.author: Devin Kelly
items.quote: Do not mock them for their gentleness, they have a muscle that loves being alive.
items.hook: Finding profound meaning in a simple poem about clams.

items.title: Mary Oliver's "Some Questions You Might Ask"
items.publication: Ordinary Plots: Meditations on Poems + Verse
items.author: Devin Kelly
items.quote: Is the soul solid, like iron? Or is it tender and breakable, like the wings of a moth in the beak of the owl?
items.hook: Explore the soul's nature through Mary Oliver's poetic questions.

items.title: Mary O’Malley’s “Holy”
items.publication: Ordinary Plots: Meditations on Poems + Verse
items.author: Devin Kelly
items.quote: I will remember what is holy. I will say the word without shame.
items.hook: Exploring the holiness in everyday moments through poetry and parenthood.

items.title: Maya C. Popa's "Had We But World Enough"
items.publication: Ordinary Plots: Meditations on Poems + Verse
items.author: Devin Kelly
items.quote: I’m relenting, life: It’s always you who wins, and we keep living.
items.hook: A meditation on poetry and life's beauty through Maya C. Popa's work.

items.title: Michael Bazzett's "The Man Kept Reaching"
items.publication: Ordinary Plots: Meditations on Poems + Verse
items.author: Devin Kelly
items.quote: I love a prize that centers voices speaking from the other side of a half century. We live in this moment of 30 under 30 lists and all sorts of things that put pressure on young people to refine and present themselves in such a way that allows them to reach some semblance of fame or prestige or notoriety before it seems like it is too late.
items.hook: Exploring the surreal pursuit of the unattainable in poetry

items.title: Mikko Harvey's "For M"
items.publication: Ordinary Plots: Meditations on Poems + Verse
items.author: Devin Kelly
items.quote: I don’t want you to be nervous. Maybe thinking of a walrus would help. Have you seen the video of the penguin accidentally stepping on a sleeping walrus? It thought it was a rock. The walrus wakes up like what the fuck and the penguin scurries off like oh shit.
items.hook: Exploring tenderness and surprise in Mikko Harvey's poetry.

items.title: Naomi Shihab Nye's "The Art of Disappearing"
items.publication: Ordinary Plots: Meditations on Poems + Verse
items.author: Devin Kelly
items.quote:
When they say Don't I know you? say no.

When they invite you to the party remember what parties are like before answering. Someone telling you in a loud voice they once wrote a poem. Greasy sausage balls on a paper plate. Then reply.
items.hook: Discover the art of disappearing into your own world.

items.title: Norman Dubie's "A Grandfather's Last Letter"
items.publication: Ordinary Plots: Meditations on Poems + Verse
items.author: Devin Kelly
items.quote: The very young and old are best at finding Little things to do. The world is jealous of us, you know?
items.hook: A grandfather's tender letter explores life's wonders and mysteries.

items.title: Phillip B. Williams' "Paradise"
items.publication: Ordinary Plots: Meditations on Poems + Verse
items.author: Devin Kelly
items.quote: The repetition of sameness over time allows such sameness to begin to strike a different note, to reveal, to clarify, but only if you listen.
items.hook: Explore how repetition in poetry can transform language and evoke collective experience.

items.title: Rachel Zucker's "Hours Days Years Unmoor Their Orbits"
items.publication: Ordinary Plots: Meditations on Poems + Verse
items.author: Devin Kelly
items.quote: Both today’s poem and the one I just mentioned perform an act of holding in the midst of all of that forgetting.
items.hook: Exploring how poetry transforms our understanding of time and love.

items.title: Ron Padgett's "In Fact"
items.publication: Ordinary Plots: Meditations on Poems + Verse
items.author: Devin Kelly
items.quote: It’s not a poetry of escape, Padgett’s poetry, but rather a poetry of staying put, briefly, in this brief thing we call a life.
items.hook: Exploring gendered criticism and the treatment of emotionality in literature.

items.title: Sanna Wani’s “What I Thought Love Was”
items.publication: Ordinary Plots: Meditations on Poems + Verse
items.author: Devin Kelly
items.quote: Love, instead, as the way there, with the billboards and the tall grass rushing past in the periphery as the road ahead seems to curve with such slowness that it seems to move almost away from you, over the edge of the earth, even as you move toward it.
items.hook: Exploring love through the lens of poetry and the ordinary.

items.title: Tove Ditlevsen’s “My Best Time” (translated by Sophia Hersi Smith & Jennifer Russell)
items.publication: Ordinary Plots: Meditations on Poems + Verse
items.author: Devin Kelly
items.quote: And I am of no use unlike people out there, but in my mind's dark refuge something is renewed— and something knotted daily is soundlessly undone as a branch at dawn sways in a bird's wake.
items.hook: Exploring solitude and childhood in Tove Ditlevsen's 'My Best Time'.

items.title: A poem by Derek Chan
items.author: Oxford Poetry
items.quote: I mourn you now despite not knowing who I am. I mourn this moment despite standing in the future where there is already too much light to ignore.
items.hook: Mourning the unknown and the future in vivid, poetic imagery.

items.title: A poem by Hua Xi
items.quote: You answer the phone in the ﬁrst person even though you are only snow falling.
items.hook: A haunting poem about communication and loss.

items.title: A poem by Margaret Atwood
items.quote: Maybe I’ll make something of them, these little scraps of fabric abandoned in their drawers, these buttons, fallen from vanished shirts I mended once, with care – these little words I tucked away for later.
items.hook: Crafting new beginnings from the remnants of the past.

items.title: A poem by Rowan Ricardo Phillips
items.author: Oxford Poetry
items.quote: The thought comes sharp at first, Then room tone – The motor in the refrigerator, The faint pressure of air on your skin Forgotten until the wind rises.
items.hook: Exploring the cyclical nature of life and thought through lyrical beauty.

items.title: A poem by Sinéad Morrissey
items.author: Oxford Poetry
items.quote: The runway, an immensity of permissible trespass, is performing its own apotheosis as Berliners hardier than us pound round its lots.
items.hook: A family's summer in Berlin, exploring survival and memory.

items.title: For human dignity
items.author: Philosophy bear
items.quote: Near constant, almost unimaginable agony is the only summary, and when I considered the condition as a whole, the response was: just let me die, please just let me die.
items.hook: Discover the profound struggle for human dignity amidst suffering.

items.title: For more lifeboats: The only just academic job market is a tight academic job market
items.author: Philosophy bear
items.quote: The justest job markets we have are tight job markets. Tight job markets give second chances for those left behind through unfair disadvantages, tight job markets tend to equalise wages, tight job markets make companies treat their employees right, and make it more difficult for employers to use sexism etc. to their advantage.
items.hook: A tighter academic job market is more just and equitable.

items.title: Harm OCD, a brief introduction
items.author: Philosophy bear
items.quote: Having an intrusive thought about doing x does not mean you are tempted to do x. Quite the opposite, it means that you find x especially abhorrent or terrifying.
items.hook: Discover why intrusive thoughts don't mean temptation in Harm OCD.

items.title: How I would like to live
items.author: Philosophy bear
items.quote: I cut off the top of my skull and set it down as a great cauldron, large enough to hold an ocean. This is necessary because the energies of my being are now oceanic in scale (could any human be otherwise?) I prepare the four feasts for the four sets of guests roughly in line with the tradition. I am fed to the beings of the universe.
items.hook: Explore self-sacrifice and fear through Tibetan Chod meditation.

items.title: Property, democracy and automation: pick two
items.author: Philosophy bear
items.quote: The public will be aware these factors no longer hold - it will be obvious. Thus, they will have every incentive to expropriate all private property in large productive assets- if they still have the capacity to do so.
items.hook: Can democracy survive in a fully automated world?

items.title: Punishment abolitionism
items.author: Philosophy bear
items.quote: I believe I dislike both prisons and punishment far more than some of those who call themselves prison abolitionists. Prison abolitionism arises from noble instincts, but much of what goes under the name is a flawed instrument. It can be gestural, content at the expression of sentiment and proud not to think in specificities.
items.hook: Why prison abolitionism isn't enough

items.title: The Mystery of Love
items.author: Philosophy bear
items.quote: The first thing to understand about the song is that three of its characters- Rogue River, the narrator’s lover, and God become symbolically identified with each other. The song is very clear about this identification- it’s not something you have to strain to see. Once you do see it, the song begins to disclose itself to you.
items.hook: Explore the unity of opposites in Sufjan Stevens' 'The Mystery of Love'

items.title: The Accusation of Fantasy
items.author: Peter Hague
items.quote: There is no reasonable well-informed observer who would consider O’Neill ‘nutty’ - he was a well-regarded Princeton professor, and his ideas had been developed under the constraints of good mathematics, physics and engineering.
items.hook: Why are visionary ideas often dismissed as fantasies?

items.title: What if we kissed in the abandoned GameStop?
items.author: Sam Kriss
items.quote: This store was boarded up when you arrived, but everything inside is still pristine. In the dead malls the lights shine evenly and the acres of grey carpeting unroll smooth between empty shelves. This is the beige inferno.
items.hook: Discover the haunting beauty of abandoned malls.

items.title: Are parents better people?
items.author: Paul Bloom
items.quote: The future is a foreign country. If my children are there, I do not want their lives to be ravaged by war, famine, or poverty. And so I want things to turn out better for everyone.
items.hook: Does having children make people more empathetic or selfless?

items.title: Do doomers believe what they say?
items.author: Paul Bloom
items.quote: Unless doomers act in ways consistent with their doomer views, it’s fair to assume that they don’t really believe what they’re saying.
items.hook: Exploring the gap between doomers' predictions and their personal actions.

items.title: How to give a better-than-average talk
items.author: Paul Bloom
items.quote: The audience is your friend. They want you to give a good talk. This is because most people are kind, and also because a good talk is in their own interests.
items.hook: Transform your public speaking skills with practical, insightful advice.

items.title: Immortality Sounds Pretty Good, Actually
items.author: Paul Bloom
items.quote: If you enjoy life right now, why not get more of it? Duh.
items.hook: Defending the idea of living indefinitely against philosophical objections.

items.title: Is parenthood selfish or selfless? It’s both.
items.author: Paul Bloom
items.quote: Indeed, some scientists, like Israeli psychologist Ruth Feldman, have argued that our very notion of empathy originates from the evolutionary foundations of parenthood.
items.hook: Exploring how parenthood shapes empathy and self-interest.

items.title: Art of Darkness
items.author: Maia Mindel
items.quote: The concept of a pigment that could only be used by one person was very controversial, much to the chagrin of SNS - they struck numerous deals with various private companies for the exclusive rights to Vantablack.
items.hook: Can you own a color? Explore the controversy and rationale behind color ownership.

items.title: This Land Is Our Land
items.author: Maia Mindel
items.quote: The paradox over who is the rightful owner of the land, the people who’ve worked it since time immemorial or the people who have a legal claim built on coercion, is central to the problems with the thought of one of Strauss’s targets, John Locke.
items.hook: Explore the paradox of land ownership and justice.

items.title: Why "Why Nations Fail" Fails
items.author: Maia Mindel
items.quote: A clear example of the thin and the contextual nature of inclusive vs extractive institutions can be found in the two main forms of exploitation of the native Peruvian population by the Spanish: mita and encomienda.
items.hook: Explore the nuanced critique of 'Why Nations Fail' and its thesis on institutions.

items.title: Can we be certain that time really exists?
items.author: Starts With A Bang
items.quote: When it comes to the question of existence, physics is very simple and straightforward about what it considers to be a satisfactory answer.
items.hook: Explore the philosophical and scientific questions about the existence of time.

items.title: Cosmic birefringence: the signal that could upend cosmology
items.author: Starts With A Bang
items.quote: However, it’s important to check the CMB’s light for those effects, because there are three main explanations for cosmic birefringence if we do, indeed, observe it.
items.hook: Discover cosmic birefringence and its potential to reshape cosmology.

items.title: Do we live inside a baby universe that’s really a black hole on the outside?
items.author: Starts With A Bang
items.quote: Remarkably, the Schwarzschild radius of a black hole with the mass of all the matter in the observable Universe is almost exactly equal to the observed size of the visible Universe!
items.hook: Could our Universe be inside a black hole?

items.title: Flying through time
items.author: Starts With A Bang
items.quote: If light’s polarization is inherently rotated, even by a fraction of a degree, it could reveal a preferred direction in the Universe, pointing to exotic new physics or even a flaw in our cosmic picture.
items.hook: Discover how cosmic birefringence could challenge our understanding of the universe.

items.title: The Universe has changed by the time you finish this sentence
items.author: Starts With A Bang
items.quote: But all of these events take time: enormous amounts of time. Stars occasionally pass through our Oort Cloud, but that only happens a couple of times every million years. The Sun will continue burning for 5-7 billion more years before it evolves to the next stage of its life.
items.hook: Discover how the universe changes in just three seconds.

items.title: Owning Our Words: Sounding the Depths of Language
items.author: L. M. Sacasas
items.quote: Words are the most subtle symbols which we possess and our human fabric depends on them. The living and radical nature of language is something which we forget at our peril.
items.hook: Explore how language shapes human flourishing and responsibility.

items.title: Waiting Is a Revelation
items.author: L. M. Sacasas
items.quote: Waiting is not a passage of time to be traversed but a condition of our being … an opportunity to encounter those aspects of life deeply, perhaps neurotically, hidden in our busyness. In waiting, in listening to the inward melody of duration, we become attuned to our being." — Harold Schweizer, “On Waiting
items.hook: Reframe waiting as a life-giving experience.

items.title: What Did We Lose When We Lost the Stars?
items.author: L. M. Sacasas
items.quote: Seen in this light, our own relationship to the night sky appears as a remarkable, and perhaps tragic, anomaly.
items.hook: Explore the cultural loss of the night sky due to modern technology.

items.title: Age of Invention: Does History have a Replication Crisis?
items.publication: Age of Invention, by Anton Howes
items.author: Anton Howes
items.quote: Historical myths, often based on mere misunderstanding, but occasionally on bias or fraud, spread like wildfire. People just love to share unusual and interesting facts, and history is replete with things that are both unusual and true.
items.hook: Why do historical myths persist despite being debunked?

items.title: Age of Invention: How to be a Public Historian
items.publication: Age of Invention, by Anton Howes
items.author: Anton Howes
items.quote: But as Ferriss notes, it’s a Faustian bargain. Just through sheer numbers alone, if your work reaches an audience the size of a city, or perhaps even a small country, then it will inevitably reach a lot of people who are simply mad, bad or sad.
items.hook: The Faustian bargain of reaching a massive audience

items.title: Age of Invention: Joel Mokyr's Nobel
items.publication: Age of Invention, by Anton Howes
items.author: Anton Howes
items.quote: Mokyr’s is the economic history that gets written up in books – his classics are The Lever of Riches, The Gifts of Athena, The Enlightened Economy, and A Culture of Growth – and in readable papers shorn of unnecessary formulae.
items.hook: Discover how ideas fueled the Industrial Revolution.

items.title: Age of Invention: Just Kiln Time
items.publication: Age of Invention, by Anton Howes
items.author: Anton Howes
items.quote: The kiln worked as follows. Once the germinating grain had been drained of its excess water, the maltster spread it evenly across a haircloth, which was placed on a mat woven of straw, wicker, or thin wooden splints.
items.hook: Discover how maltsters revolutionized brewing with smokeless kilns.

items.title: Age of Invention: The Coal Conquest
items.publication: Age of Invention, by Anton Howes
items.author: Anton Howes
items.quote: And yet the deforestation thesis simply does not work. In fact it makes no sense at all.
items.hook: Discover why Britain switched from wood to coal despite abundant forests.

items.title: Age of Invention: The Dutch Salten Age
items.publication: Age of Invention, by Anton Howes
items.author: Anton Howes
items.quote: The Dutch, by the 1440s, had thus gained a share of the carrying trade, exchanging Atlantic bay salt for the Baltic’s grain, timber, and various naval stores like hemp for rope and pitch for caulking.
items.hook: Discover how the Dutch transformed salt trade in the Baltic.

items.title: Being John Rawls
items.author: Scott Alexander
items.quote: My theory of charity,” said John Rawls Visionary, “centers on nine words: there but for the grace of God go I. Society is a contract where we agree to help the less fortunate, knowing that if the shoe were on the other foot, they would help us in turn.
items.hook: A theory of charity based on mutual aid and moral character.

items.title: Rather Better Pasturage for Their Cows
items.author: Henry Oliver
items.quote: When we laugh with her, she is preparing us for a more permanent and persistent joy.
items.hook: Rediscover Jane Austen's novels as joyful romances, not just social critiques.

items.title: What is literary criticism if it is not close reading? Art, Magic, and Common Sense.
items.author: Henry Oliver
items.quote: The magic of poetry is the way that it can create a new sense of the world—can make you believe in things not merely unbelievable, but which we know to be untrue. The art of poetry is in the specific wording of the spell—change the words, get the order wrong, and the magic will not manifest.
items.hook: Exploring the dual nature of poetry: art and magic.

items.title: Writing advice is a lie.
items.author: Henry Oliver
items.quote: Grammar is logic. Sound is married to sense. That paragraph works because it embodies what it says!
items.hook: Discover why conventional writing advice often misses the mark.

items.title: Everything Is Signaling
items.author: David Pinsof
items.quote: Politics is not about policy. Charity is not about helping. Art is not about insight. Education is not about learning.
items.hook: Politics, charity, art, and education are about signaling, not their apparent purposes.

items.title: Happiness Is Bullshit
items.author: David Pinsof
items.quote: The truth is, we’re animals—specifically, apes. Our brains are the product of evolution. It would be very strange if evolution made us want happiness as our number one goal. Happiness is inside our heads—it’s not out there in the world. It has no connection to survival or reproduction, which kind of has to exist if we evolved to want it.
items.hook: Happiness isn't our ultimate goal; primal desires drive us.

items.title: Utilitarianism Is Bullshit
items.author: David Pinsof
items.quote: What we’re pursuing is not good vibes in our heads, but the (often unflattering) things in the world that evolution programmed us to pursue, like sex, status, yummies, moral superiority, and high-status offspring.
items.hook: Rethinking happiness and suffering through evolutionary psychology.

items.title: 28 slightly rude notes on writing
items.author: Adam Mastroianni
items.quote: All writing about despair is ultimately insincere. Putting fingers to keys or pen to paper is secretly an act of hope, however faint—hope that someone will read your words, hope that someone will understand. Someone who truly feels despair wouldn’t bother to tell anyone about it because they wouldn’t expect it to do anything.
items.hook: Writing about despair is an act of hope.

items.title: Face it: you're a crazy person
items.author: Adam Mastroianni
items.quote: When you fully unpack any job, you’ll discover something astounding: only a crazy person should do it.
items.hook: Discover why only a 'crazy person' should pursue certain careers.

items.title: How to be less awkward
items.author: Adam Mastroianni
items.quote: Awkwardness puts a persistent bit of distance between us and the good life, like being celiac in a world where every dish has a dash of gluten in it.
items.hook: Discover why awkwardness is not a moral failing, but a complex, layered phenomenon.

items.title: I like 'em thick
items.author: Adam Mastroianni
items.quote: Great works of fiction—for that matter, great works of any art—unfurl in response to your attention. The more time you spend with them, the more you get out of them.
items.hook: Discover why great art requires time and attention to reveal its depth.

items.title: Incentives are for losers
items.author: Adam Mastroianni
items.quote: There’s a point here that should go without saying, but instead it has simply gone unsaid. Which is: incentives are for losers. Doing something simply because an arbitrary reward system will give you a lil treat—that’s for pigeons, not people. If you build your life around satisfying incentives, then you’re a dummy and a schmuck.
items.hook: Incentives are for losers: a call to rethink motivation

items.title: Nothing ever dies. It merely becomes embarrassing.
items.author: Adam Mastroianni
items.quote: We need a different approach. And so we must turn, as we so often do, to the source of all truly important ideas in the philosophy of science: the sci-fi universe of Halo.
items.hook: Why debunked psychological theories persist like Spartans in Halo.

items.title: So you wanna de-bog yourself
items.author: Adam Mastroianni
items.quote: Being stuck is the psychological equivalent of standing knee-deep in a fetid bog, bog in every direction, bog as far as the eye can see. You go wading in search of dry land and only find more bog.
items.hook: Discover the psychological bog of feeling stuck and how to escape it.

items.title: Stop eating Lady Gaga's Oreos
items.author: Adam Mastroianni
items.quote: The only thing that’s unprecedented about these craven cash-ins is how well they seem to be working. Selling out no longer carries a stigma—if anything, fans are excited for tie-ins between their favorite bands and their favorite brands, no matter how shameless.
items.hook: Why do fans love band-branded products?

items.title: The Decline of Deviance
items.author: Adam Mastroianni
items.quote: When you put all the data together, you see a stark shift in society that is on the one hand miraculous, fantastic, worthy of a ticker-tape parade. And a shift that is, on the other hand, dismal, depressing, and in need of immediate intervention.
items.hook: Discover why society's weirdness is disappearing

items.title: The Decline of Deviance 2
items.author: Adam Mastroianni
items.quote: The internet gives every social trend a pair of rocket-powered roller skates, speeding it toward its crablike final form.
items.hook: How prosperity and the internet shape cultural trends.

items.title: The rise and fall of peer review
items.author: Adam Mastroianni
items.quote: This was a massive change. From antiquity to modernity, scientists wrote letters and circulated monographs, and the main barriers stopping them from communicating their findings were the cost of paper, postage, or a printing press, or on rare occasions, the cost of a visit from the Catholic Church.
items.hook: Discover why peer review, once hailed as a scientific safeguard, may have failed.

items.title: There is no epidemic of loneliness, but there is an epidemic of scurvy
items.author: Adam Mastroianni
items.quote: We’ve got a puzzle here. People are more alone than ever, but they’re not feeling much lonelier than they used to. So maybe all this extra solitude is...fine?
items.hook: Discover why loneliness isn't the real epidemic.

items.title: Underrated ways to change the world
items.author: Adam Mastroianni
items.quote: Money, power, and selflessness are all useful tools in the right hands, but the world is messed up in all sorts of ways that can’t be legislated against, bought off, or undone with a hunger strike.
items.hook: Discover unconventional paths to making the world better.

items.title: Analytic vs Conventional Bioethics
items.author: Richard Y Chappell
items.quote: To know whether a project is good or bad, it isn’t enough to know that its proponents intend a better future. You need to know something about what, concretely, they propose to do.
items.hook: Rethink bioethics: intentions vs. actions

items.title: Hard Questions Aren’t Hopeless
items.author: Richard Y Chappell
items.quote: Philosophical cluelessness, by contrast, commits one to the much stronger claim that nobody can (realistically) form any reasonable judgments or expectations about this question, no matter how carefully they investigate it. That’s an extremely strong skeptical claim!
items.hook: Why philosophical cluelessness doesn't prevent reasonable judgments.

items.title: Puzzles for Everyone
items.author: Richard Y Chappell
items.quote: Their error, of course, is that beneficence and decision theory are essential components of any complete moral theory.
items.hook: Explore why ethical puzzles aren't just for utilitarians.

items.title: Refusing to Quantify is Refusing to Think
items.author: Richard Y Chappell
items.quote: Quantification enables large-scale comparison, and such comparison is needed in order to make high-stakes tradeoffs in an informed way. Tradeoffs, in turn, are essential to practical rationality. We can’t avoid them: different values are in conflict, and can’t all be jointly satisfied. We have to choose, or “trade off”, between them.
items.hook: Why quantifying moral decisions is essential for effective altruism

items.title: The Schmotte-and-Bailey Fallacy
items.author: Richard Y Chappell
items.quote: One way to do that is to set aside the EA truism (what I call beneficentrism) and engage with a more extreme—and hence reasonably disputable—alternative view instead.
items.hook: Discover the 'schmotte-and-bailey fallacy' in moral debates.

items.title: The Train to Crazy Town
items.author: Richard Y Chappell
items.quote: As a first step, I want to highlight how important it is that people feel free to not act on their beliefs. It might not sound ideal, but it’s a practical guardrail that’s essential for protecting unbiased inquiry.
items.hook: Explore how moral theories guide actions without constraining beliefs.

items.title: What is Unjust Discrimination?
items.author: Richard Y Chappell
items.quote: To a first approximation, I think we unjustly discriminate when we unjustifiably discount someone’s interests for morally irrelevant reasons (such as demographic categories).
items.hook: Explore why disparate impact alone doesn't define unjust discrimination.

items.title: Why You Are An NPC
items.author: Gurwinder
items.quote: In 2016 a team of physicists led by Lachlan Gunn investigated the accuracy of witnesses picking suspects from police lineups. They found that as the size of unanimous agreement increased, so did its inaccuracy, until it was no better than chance.
items.hook: Discover why unanimous agreement often signals a lack of independent thinking.

items.title: On child birth
items.author: Henrik Karlsson
items.quote: Giving birth is the most painful thing I’ve ever been through. And it’s a very particular kind of pain: that you stand there waiting for the contractions. You know it’s coming, this pain that just fills you to the brim. It is coming, again and again. And you have to face the pain, you have to turn toward it, you can’t look away.
items.hook: How mindset and oxytocin shape childbirth experiences.

items.title: Some remarks on being stuck, with digressions on David Hockney, developing style, and gardens
items.author: Henrik Karlsson
items.quote: The problem with his old images, and with photography, was that that is not at all what the world looks like to us. And with this articulation, he was able to delineate what was to become the main project of the second half of the career, namely, as I said: finding ways of making pictures that are more true to how we see the world than photography is.
items.hook: Exploring how artists break free from conventional perspectives

items.title: First we shape our feedback loops; then they shape us
items.author: Henrik Karlsson
items.quote: The deeper lesson here is not that indexing your journal will make you a better writer. It might; I don’t know. The lesson is that the feedback loops that we let work on ourselves shape us to an unsettling degree.
items.hook: How feedback loops shape your writing and self-awareness

items.title: Sometimes the reason you can’t find people you resonate with is because you misread the ones you meet
items.author: Henrik Karlsson
items.quote: The third and deepest kinds of friendship, according to Aristotle, is a friendship of virtue. That is, you like a person because of their character. They might be fun, they might be useful, but even if they aren’t, you like them anyway.
items.hook: Discover the enduring power of friendships of virtue.

items.title: Some relationships deepen when you tell the truth and some end
items.author: Henrik Karlsson
items.quote: When you prioritize what you yourself value, everything around you shifts, and asserting that value creates a kind of gravitational pull on the world so that things, systems, relationships get a chance to find new arrangements.
items.hook: How does prioritizing personal values reshape relationships?

items.title: Cultivating a state of mind where new ideas are born
items.author: Henrik Karlsson
items.quote: Good ideas — actually, no, great ideas are fragile. Great ideas are easy to kill. An idea in its larval stage — all the best ideas when I first heard them sound bad. And all of us, myself included, are much more affected by what other people think of us and our ideas than we like to admit.
items.hook: How solitude fosters groundbreaking ideas

items.title: Love is about being invested in someone’s continual expansion
items.author: Henrik Karlsson
items.quote: Being young and lost, we made our relationship into a cocoon, a place where we felt safe enough to… well, what is it that caterpillars do in cocoons really? Dissolve themselves into a nutritious soup and assemble a new self.
items.hook: Discover how love fuels personal growth and transformation.

items.title: Relationships are coevolutionary loops
items.author: Henrik Karlsson
items.quote:
A polaroid photo by Andrei Tarkvosky

“Dependence is scorned even in intimate relationships, as though dependence were incompatible with self-reliance rather than the only thing that makes it possible.”
― Maggie Nelson, The Argonauts
items.hook: Discover how relationships evolve like nature's coevolutionary loops.

items.title: The world reveals itself to those who travel by foot
items.author: Henrik Karlsson
items.quote: The world (like people!) grows bigger, more varied, and interesting if I’m open, playful, and trusting.
items.hook: How travel and friendships can expand your world view.

items.title: Everything that turned out well in my life followed the same design process
items.author: Henrik Karlsson
items.quote: I paid attention to things I liked to do, and found ways to do more of that. I made it easy for interesting people to find me, and then I hung out with them. We did projects together.
items.hook: Discover how aligning life with context leads to success.

items.title: Notes on Acquired Taste
items.author: Ian Leslie
items.quote: Taste is similarly post-rationalised, or back-propagated. You notice what you like or dislike and extract a rule from your response. Do this enough times and you build a powerful discrimination engine.
items.hook: Explore how taste evolves and shapes human culture.

items.title: The Banality of Genius: Notes on Peter Jackson's Get Back
items.author: Ian Leslie
items.quote: Immersed in all this banality, a funny thing happens to the viewer. As we get into the rhythm of the Beatles’ daily lives, we start to inhabit their world.
items.hook: Discover how The Beatles' mundane moments reveal their creative genius.

items.title: Why Does Every Society Invent the Same Things?
items.author: Ian Leslie
items.quote: The pleasure of rhythmic music is a happy side-effect of our adaptation for language.
items.hook: Why do humans universally invent similar cultural practices?

items.title: Agonistes
items.author: Alistair Kitchen
items.quote: His envisaged death offered him the measure of how intolerable his life would be if he accepted the intolerable condition of the world as it is. His envisaged death offered him the measure of the necessity of changing the world. It was by the license granted him by his envisaged death that he was able to live with the necessary pride that becomes a man.
items.hook: Explore the moral courage of Che Guevara and the philosophy of intolerability.

items.title: Contra Ganz on Guns
items.author: Alistair Kitchen
items.quote: The mere presence of guns, on the other hand, is a reminder that guns can, even should, be used. It is their raison d’etre.
items.hook: How gun accessibility shapes American psychology and violence.

items.title: Liberated Zone
items.author: Alistair Kitchen
items.quote: The performance had to me the uneasy feel of the first stages of a bullfight. First, a loud device, usually a trumpet, announces the start of the show. The participants then parade into the arena, displaying themselves and their fancy outfits to the audience. They always move with a kind of camp arrogance.
items.hook: A university protest as a bullfight: authority, protest, and absurdity.

items.title: Liberated Zone VII
items.author: Alistair Kitchen
items.quote: Individual donors clearly do exert power over university presidents: the mystery is how. And I think the most plausible explanation is that, in the political economy of the university system, material factors take a back seat in determining power relations.
items.hook: How do individual donors wield power over university decisions?

items.title: The new female contempt
items.author: Alistair Kitchen
items.quote: Women have gained the bravado and the platforms to speak publicly about men in the way that men have traditionally often spoken about women—with contempt.
items.hook: Explore the reversal of gender roles in social contempt.

items.title: The only show in town
items.author: Alistair Kitchen
items.quote: The peasants of Europe and the citizens of Hiroshima/Nagasaki had no say over what happened to them. Nor did the European nobles, for that matter, or Emperor Hirohito, the POWs on the Burmese railway, or the slaves of the Caribbean.
items.hook: How global events shape lives beyond borders

items.title: Contra Weisenthal on Highways
items.author: Maxwell Tabarrok
items.quote: But the welfare gains from building houses remain. Although every consumer is indifferent to the supply shift and ends up paying the same price, just like with the new lane, the economy enjoys net welfare gains because those consumer’s rent payments aren’t just dissipated resources.
items.hook: Why building houses raises welfare even if prices don't drop

items.title: Does Economics Flip-flop on the Minimum Wage?
items.author: Maxwell Tabarrok
items.quote: The competitive search equilibrium is consistent with the empirical evidence (including the randomized control trials on the minimum wage) and it preserves the signs of the econ 101 comparative statics on the minimum wage. Unemployment goes up and deadweight loss is created.
items.hook: Explore how monopsony and search costs reshape the minimum wage debate.

items.title: Don't Endorse the Idea of Market Failure
items.author: Maxwell Tabarrok
items.quote: It’s not unique to pollution or climate change either. Governments massively underfund research and development despite it being the world’s most important positive externality. Governments impose huge negative externalities across borders with tariffs and immigration restrictions.
items.hook: Questioning the role of government in correcting market failures.

items.title: Is The Great Stagnation Actually Just a 'So-So' Stagnation?
items.author: Maxwell Tabarrok
items.quote: If this story is true, and more education hasn’t been raising productivity, then all the GDP growth we thought was due to more skilled workers is actually coming from somewhere else. That means we’ve been undercounting TFP, and technological progress for decades.
items.hook: Reevaluating the true source of GDP growth beyond education

items.title: The Causal Effect of Income is (Often) Zero
items.author: Maxwell Tabarrok
items.quote: The causal effect of wealth on mortality is zero. That means that if you took someone from the poorer cohort, who is 2% more likely to die than someone with $140k in extra cash and you gave them $140,000, they would still be 2% more likely to die than the people who started with that money.
items.hook: Extra income doesn't necessarily improve health or longevity.

items.title: The Puzzle of Historical Preservation
items.author: Maxwell Tabarrok
items.quote: This is the puzzle: why did completely uncontrolled building lead to beautiful places in the past but seems unlikely to do the same today?
items.hook: Why did uncontrolled building create beauty in the past?

items.title: The Timeless Way of Building
items.author: Maxwell Tabarrok
items.quote: The patterns that define a building, or a city, or a life, arise from the events which keep on happening there most often.
items.hook: Discover how patterns shape our buildings and cities.

items.title: Alchemy is ok
items.author: Ethan Ludwin-Peery
items.quote: We need a paradigm to give us shape and turn us into a mature science. No number of discoveries, however robust or interesting to non-specialists, can make that happen.
items.hook: Discover how alchemy's discoveries parallel modern psychology's quest for a paradigm.

items.title: How to Market Hampshire College
items.author: Ethan Ludwin-Peery
items.quote: Hampshire is the greatest model of higher education ever invented, and I don’t care who knows it.
items.hook: Discover why Hampshire College is the greatest model of higher education.

items.title: Real Hampshire College Has Never Been Tried
items.author: Ethan Ludwin-Peery
items.quote: We can relaunch Hampshire with the financial foundation the original institution never had, and prove that this model is viable when properly managed.
items.hook: Revive a unique college model with a solid financial foundation.

items.title: REPOST: What You Want from Tests
items.author: Ethan Ludwin-Peery
items.quote: Tests have some natural strengths and some obvious weaknesses. If we understand these strengths and weaknesses, we can design tests that let us meet more of our goals.
items.hook: Rethinking the role of tests in education

items.title: Study the Self-Evident
items.author: Ethan Ludwin-Peery
items.quote: The task is not to see what has never been seen before, but to think what has never been thought before about what you see everyday.
items.hook: Rethink the obvious to unlock scientific insights.

items.title: Why Psychology Hasn’t Had a Big New Idea in Decades
items.author: Ethan Ludwin-Peery
items.quote: A science needs a paradigm because we underrate a simple fact: there are an infinite number of things you can study and infinite ways to study them.
items.hook: How does psychology's lack of a paradigm affect its progress?

items.title: Morality without skyhooks
items.author: Lionel Page
items.quote: In truth, most of us would struggle to articulate a meaningful answer to such a disarming toddler. In fact, many professional philosophers would too.
items.hook: Exploring morality without relying on ungrounded explanations.

items.title: The truth about happiness
items.author: Lionel Page
items.quote: Happiness is an affective state that motivates us to engage in actions that are likely to lead to outcomes that would, on average, lead to increases in the likelihood of survival and/or reproduction.
items.hook: Rethinking happiness through evolution and neuroscience

items.title: Aliens Are Not Crazy Unlikely
items.author: Robin Hanson
items.quote: But as an author of the great filter and grabby aliens analysis, I say that I’m a world class expert on the prior for this hypothesis. The possibility that some-UFOs-are-aliens is completely consistent with all known physical, biological, and social laws.
items.hook: Rethinking the likelihood of extraterrestrial life and UFOs

items.title: My Status Circles
items.author: Robin Hanson
items.quote: So I very much respect folks who deliberately try to, and successfully do, make progress on important neglected topics.
items.hook: Explore how intellectual circles value original insight over fame.

items.title: No-New-Physics Consciousness
items.author: Robin Hanson
items.quote: The obvious simple local rule to consider re which experiences systems actually feel is something like panpsychism: all experience systems made of brains that calculate what they would feel, if they were to feel, actually do feel that feeling.
items.hook: Exploring consciousness through the lens of physics and philosophy.

items.title: The Arc of Moral Authority: From Tradition To Interiors To Prices
items.author: Robin Hanson
items.quote: For the post-modern era, the process solutions that I’ve found to cultural drift are (a) letting capitalism run everything, (b) groups managed to raise futures market price estimates of future group adaptive success, and (c) large regions managed to improve futures market estimates of dates when we achieve sacred goals that conflict with civ collapse.
items.hook: Discover how speculative market prices could become the new moral authority.

items.title: The Modern Mind's Fatal Flaw
items.author: Robin Hanson
items.quote: We’ve been assuming that the goals in our heads are coherent and stable, and could serve as the basis for a functioning civilization of artificial minds and global governance. But in fact they are broken and fast decaying, and unable to support such a new civilization.
items.hook: How modern cultural evolution threatens future civilizations

items.title: Your Conscience Is Not A Moral Oracle
items.author: Robin Hanson
items.quote: We must accept that moral truth is not something that any of us have much direct evidence on, beyond the easy truth that suffering tends to be bad.
items.hook: Rethink the role of conscience in moral judgment.

items.title: how to begin
items.author: Celine Nguyen
items.quote: Copying teaches technique and taste. It works for design and writing and many other disciplines. But with writing, I find that faithfully copying a work isn’t as instructive. What seems to be more useful is an approach I’ve been thinking of as ‘deep copying.’
items.hook: Discover the art of 'deep copying' to enhance your writing craft.

items.title: no one told me about proust
items.author: Celine Nguyen
items.quote: An hour is not just an hour, it is a vessel full of perfumes, sounds, plans and atmospheres.
items.hook: Discover how Proust reshaped one reader's understanding of literature and life.

items.title: the life you were meant to live
items.author: Celine Nguyen
items.quote: It seems, initially, like this is the right move for the Wheelers. And as Frank looks back at his life, he thinks: Wasn’t it true, then, that everything in his life from that point on had been a succession of things he hadn’t really wanted to do?
items.hook: Explore the tension between professional success and artistic fulfillment.

items.title: Apparently Criminals Don’t Have Free Will, But Elites Do
items.author: Rob Henderson
items.quote: Free will works the same way. A choice exists at the scale of a person thinking, weighing and deciding. Looking at the molecules underneath and finding no choice there doesn’t prove that choice is an illusion.
items.hook: Exploring the illusion of free will and its moral implications.

items.title: No One Expects Young Men To Do Anything and They Are Responding By Doing Nothing
items.author: Rob Henderson
items.quote: Poor behavior from young males is an important and often overlooked reason why rates of fatherless homes have increased.
items.hook: Why young men's behavior is reshaping family structures

items.title: Some Status Games Are Worth Playing
items.author: Rob Henderson
items.quote: Congleton suggests this story is too simple. Some status games are wasteful. But others produce real benefits for people who are not actually playing the game.
items.hook: Exploring the complex role of status-seeking in human behavior and society.

items.title: The Logic of Envy
items.author: Rob Henderson
items.quote: The idea is that while porn is usually thought of as a means to orgasm, this is actually a lie people tell themselves. Porn is in fact a means to deprive someone else of pleasure.
items.hook: Explore the psychological underpinnings of envy through the lens of pornography.

items.title: A Ludicrous No-Brainer
items.author: Hinternet Editorial Board
items.quote: I, JSR, have been struggling these past few months to explain, in a first instance to myself, why it has lately felt so hard to write, or to write in a way that feels adequate to our moment, that feels true.
items.hook: Why is writing so hard in the digital age?

items.title: It only snows like this for children
items.author: Erik Hoel
items.quote: Snow is the dreamworld, and so snow is death too. It’s both. The veil between worlds is thin after a snow.
items.hook: Explore how snow symbolizes the dreamworld and the passage of time.

items.title: CWD Is a Trust Test for Wildlife Agencies
items.author: Braxton McCoy
items.quote: CWD is increasingly reshaping the entire wildlife management landscape across North America.
items.hook: How CWD is reshaping wildlife management and public trust.

items.title: Owls, Sage Grouse, and Richard Nixon
items.author: Braxton McCoy
items.quote: For the first time in my life the Endangered Species Act, an important but oft times callously wielded tool, worked in practice the way it was always meant to in spirit.
items.hook: How the Endangered Species Act can balance conservation and economic interests.
